extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, legal scholars, and advanced law students interested in claim interpretation and construction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for distinguishing and applying interpretation (linguistic meaning) versus construction (legal effect) in patent-claim analysis, including standards of evidence, temporal/audience reference points, and when normative considerations may legitimately override plain meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: determine the linguistic meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation is the task of determining the linguistic meaning of text—the understanding of the text by the intended audience at the time the patent is written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the intended audience's understanding (often scientists and competitors in the relevant field) at the filing date as the reference point. The linguistic meaning is a factual question separable from legal consequences. Example: the linguistic meaning of a claim will generally be how a "person skilled in the art" would understand the claim language at the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: determine the legal scope/effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction is the activity of determining the legal meaning and effect of a text; it may or may not track the linguistic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction is irreducibly normative: judges decide what weight to give linguistic meaning and may adopt alternative reference points (e.g., the patentee's inventive idea). There are two kinds: (a) filling gaps where linguistic meaning runs out (the construction zone) and (b) adopting second-order anti-textualist theories that can override clear text. Use normative theories (utilitarian, deontological, textualist, etc.) to justify constructions and to avoid arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use person of ordinary skill in the art as interpretive standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The linguistic meaning of a claim is ordinarily the understanding of a person working in the same field as the patentee (often called a 'person skilled in the art') at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing date approximates the temporal reference. Focus on how those in the field would understand the claim language qua language (not their conception of the invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on patentee's unexpressed intent for linguistic meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic meaning does not depend on the patentee's unexpressed intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee's broad intent (to claim as much as courts will allow) renders reliance on unexpressed intent circular and unhelpful for interpretation. Avoid treating internal patentee motivations as the linguistic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate linguistic meaning with patentee's invention or legal entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation refers to how a person skilled in the art understands the claim language, not to that person's understanding of the patentee's invention or what the patentee is 'entitled' to monopolize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basing interpretation on the patentee's invention or entitlement is circular because legal entitlement is itself the construction outcome. Keep interpretation and construction analytically separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat dictionaries and expert interpreters as proxies, not definitive authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries and expert interpreters are merely proxies for a deeper inquiry into how the intended audience understands language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct evidence of linguistic usage (patterns of usage) when available. Dictionaries can be wrong or fail to capture field-specific meanings; use them as helpful but non-conclusive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both intrinsic and extrinsic evidence are relevant to interpretation and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence (specification, prosecution history) and extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) can both inform linguistic meaning and legal construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dichotomy about which is better is a red herring; treat both types as relevant but relevant in different ways to each inquiry. Do not conflate the debate into a rule that intrinsic always controls or extrinsic always controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: When linguistic evidence is unavailable, interpretation may be impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to determine the correct linguistic meaning depends on the availability of evidence (dictionaries, historical usage, expert testimony); if deep evidence of usage is not available, correct linguistic meaning may be unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits: ancient or poorly evidenced languages/usages (e.g., Code of Hammurabi) may leave interpretation indeterminate; courts then must rely on constructional choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ambiguity from vagueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity involves discrete multiple senses of a word (e.g., 'animal' can mean Animalia including humans or specifically non-human animals); vagueness involves blurred boundaries and borderline cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ambiguity as a semantic question of which discrete sense applies; vagueness requires normative line-drawing in the construction zone. Example: Martek (word 'animal') was ambiguity, not vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: If terms are vague, construction requires normative line-drawing unless a shared special meaning exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague terms (e.g., 'loud', 'near', 'about') require courts to draw a line to resolve borderline cases; such line-drawing is normative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for contextualized precise definitions shared by author and reader (a 'special understanding') that can eliminate vagueness (e.g., 'large' at McDonald's, 'high blood pressure' defined medically). Such special understandings are rare in laws of general application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize exceptional cases with no single linguistic meaning or with multiple intended meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some situations present no correct linguistic meaning (gibberish) or multiple intended/conveyed meanings (double entendre), making interpretation indeterminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such exceptional cases courts must construct legal outcomes using non-linguistic guides because linguistic meaning is real but irreducibly plural or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the interpretation-construction distinction to avoid circularity and confused argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflating linguistic meaning with legal effect collapses analysis into circular reasoning (the court 'follows meaning' where meaning is defined as the court's chosen outcome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolate linguistic meaning as a descriptive factual inquiry separate from normative construction to preserve analytic clarity and prevent using policy reasons to redefine semantic facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When construing claims, decide the weight to give linguistic meaning and select alternative lodestars if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges must first decide how much weight to give to linguistic meaning; if they do not give it weight (or if it runs out), they must adopt an alternative point of reference (e.g., patentee's inventive idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the normative justification for the choice of lodestar. If choosing the linguistic meaning, be prepared to fill gaps for vague terms; if choosing another reference, acknowledge the normative reasons for overriding textual meaning (e.g., skepticism about deference to patentee-drafted claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misdiagnosing normative disagreements as linguistic ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many disputes framed as 'ambiguity' are actually normative disagreements about whether the linguistic meaning should be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the interpretation-construction distinction to diagnose whether parties are arguing over factual semantic meaning or over competing normative theories of construction. This prevents searching for linguistic 'solutions' to essentially policy problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not default to dictionary-over-all ('dictionary uber alles')
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal dictionary definitions are not dispositive of linguistic meaning; dictionaries are learned authors' opinions and may not reflect field-specific or contextual usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess common usage among the relevant skilled audience and the patent context rather than mechanically applying dictionary definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date as temporal anchor for linguistic meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a patent is generally written just before it is filed, the filing date provides a reasonable approximation of the date by which the linguistic meaning is determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence of usage as of the filing date to evaluate how a person skilled in the art would have understood the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent examiners perform construction when assessing entitlement to issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the PTO historically claimed examiners 'interpret' claims and courts 'construe' them, examiners are effectively constructing legal effect when they decide whether a patent is legally entitled to issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that PTO decisions about claim scope for examination purposes implicate constructional judgments (legal effect), not merely neutral linguistic interpretation.
